This example tests whether independent pairs follow a bivariate Student
$t$ distribution. We fix the degrees of freedom at five and estimate two
location parameters, two diagonal dispersion entries, and one correlation.
We use the multiplier bootstrap, the default in `gof.test()`
(`simulation = "mult"`).
See the [univariate vignette](univariate.html) for an introduction to the
bootstrap procedures and p-values.

## Simulate paired observations

Let $v_1$ and $v_2$ denote the diagonal entries of the dispersion matrix.
The off-diagonal entry is $\rho\sqrt{v_1v_2}$, where $\rho$ is the
correlation. With $\nu = 5$ degrees of freedom, the covariance matrix
is $\nu/(\nu - 2)$ times the dispersion matrix.

```{r}
library(fgof)

set.seed(123)
df <- 5
location <- c(0, 1)
dispersion <- matrix(c(1, 0.6, 0.6, 2), nrow = 2)
x <- mvtnorm::rmvt(100, sigma = dispersion, df = df,
                  delta = location, type = "shifted")
```

## Supply the analytical derivatives

The multiplier bootstrap uses the derivative of the joint cumulative
distribution function (CDF) and the derivative of the log-density, also
called the score. Together they account for the effect of estimating
parameters on the fitted CDF. Each callback takes the parameter vector and
a matrix of evaluation points. It returns one row per point and one column
per estimated parameter in the order
$(\mu_1, \mu_2, v_1, v_2, \rho)$.

The callbacks below use internal `fgof` helpers through `:::`. They
capture the same fixed degrees of freedom that the test passes to the
distribution wrappers.

```{r}
cdf_gradient <- function(theta, points) {
  fgof:::gradCdfT(theta, points, df = df)
}

score <- function(theta, points) {
  fgof:::gradLogPdfT(theta, points, df = df)
}
```

## Fit the model with analytical derivatives

Use the internal `"mymvt"` distribution wrappers with `dispstr = "un"`
for unrestricted correlation. The optimizer bounds keep the diagonal
dispersion entries positive and the correlation inside $(-1, 1)$. In
two dimensions, these conditions ensure a positive definite dispersion
matrix.

```{r}
start <- list(param = c(mean(x[, 1]), mean(x[, 2]), 1, 1, 0))

set.seed(456)
fit <- gof.test(
  x, "mymvt", nsim = 199, start = start, simulation = "mult",
  derCdfWrtPar = cdf_gradient, derLogPdfWrtPar = score,
  distr.args = list(df = df, dispstr = "un"),
  optim.args = list(lower = c(-Inf, -Inf, 1e-4, 1e-4, -0.999),
                    upper = c(Inf, Inf, Inf, Inf, 0.999))
)

setNames(fit$estimate, c("mu1", "mu2", "v1", "v2", "rho"))
rbind(statistic = fit$statistic, p.value = fit$p.value)
```

## Compare with numerical derivatives

To obtain numerical derivatives for the same model, use
`numDeriv::jacobian()` on the CDF and log-density. Each Jacobian has
the same row and column order as its analytical counterpart.
As in the analytical callbacks, the degrees of freedom stay fixed.

```{r}
cdf_gradient_num <- function(theta, points) {
  numDeriv::jacobian(function(par) {
    fgof:::pmymvt(points, par, dispstr = "un", df = df)
  }, theta)
}

score_num <- function(theta, points) {
  numDeriv::jacobian(function(par) {
    fgof:::dmymvt(points, par, dispstr = "un", df = df, log = TRUE)
  }, theta)
}

theta <- fit$estimate
c(cdf = max(abs(cdf_gradient_num(theta, x) - cdf_gradient(theta, x))),
  score = max(abs(score_num(theta, x) - score(theta, x))))
```

Use the numerical callbacks in a second test and reset the seed to use
the same multiplier draws as in the analytical run.

```{r}
set.seed(456)
fit_num <- gof.test(
  x, "mymvt", nsim = 199, start = start, simulation = "mult",
  derCdfWrtPar = cdf_gradient_num, derLogPdfWrtPar = score_num,
  distr.args = list(df = df, dispstr = "un"),
  optim.args = list(lower = c(-Inf, -Inf, 1e-4, 1e-4, -0.999),
                    upper = c(Inf, Inf, Inf, Inf, 0.999))
)

rbind(analytical = fit$p.value, numerical = fit_num$p.value)
max(abs(fit$stat.sim - fit_num$stat.sim))
```

## Interpret the test statistics

For a point $(a, b)$, the joint CDF gives the probability that the first
coordinate is at most $a$ and the second is at most $b$. The test compares
this fitted probability with the observed fraction of pairs satisfying
both inequalities. By default, the multivariate test evaluates the
discrepancies at the observed pairs. The statistic `ksa` uses the largest
absolute discrepancy, and `cvma` sums squared discrepancies.
